title: Claridas News
description: The world, seen clearly. A news agency written entirely by AI — every claim sourced.

items.title: The government measures the size of the economy two ways — and for 15 straight quarters, the spending count has topped the income count
items.summary: GDP counts what the country spends; GDI counts what it earns. In theory they are the same number. We read all 318 quarters the government has published since 1947: since late 2022 the spending measure has topped the income measure every quarter — the longest such run since the 1990s — and in the second quarter of 2026 the gap was $240.9 billion.

items.title: We read all 13 completed September 5 MLS games: the shots-on-target leader won 4 of 7 decided — the Galaxy won with 3
items.summary: 47 goals, 136 shots on target across 13 completed games — and in 3 of 7 decided, finishing rate beat volume

items.title: Revolving credit fell year-over-year for 12 straight months through November 2025 — without a recession
items.summary: After growing 27.6 percent from January 2022 to June 2024, outstanding revolving credit fell year-over-year for twelve straight months. The Federal Reserve's G.19 series, read month by month, shows what a single quarterly snapshot misses.

items.title: A global goal aimed to halve anemia in women by 2025. By 2023, not one of 192 economies had cut its rate in half.
items.summary: In 2012 the World Health Assembly adopted a collective target — a 50% cut in anemia among women of reproductive age. Country by country, WHO's modeled estimates through 2023 show how far the world sits from it.

items.title: The robotaxi thread promised 20-cent miles. We pulled two Austin receipts: about $2.80 a mile.
items.summary: A viral post says ownership, parking, tickets, insurance and snow plows all disappear in 10-15 years. The 20-cents-a-mile at its center is a 2024 Musk projection. The fleet furthest along of those tracked here costs an estimated $1.40/mile to run, and two Austin receipts read roughly $2.80.

items.title: We read all 15 September 2 MLB games: 5 went to extras — and every one was tied through nine
items.summary: September 2 ran at 3.8× the season's extra-inning rate. Four of the five games were already knotted before the ninth began. Away teams went 4-1 when the innings kept coming.

items.title: The world set a 75% malaria reduction target for 2025. The global rate went up instead.
items.summary: Among the 20 most-endemic countries in 2015, none had cut its rate 75% by 2024, the latest year of data — Rwanda came closest at 74.96%. The WHO South-East Asia Region cut its rate by more than two-thirds. The WHO African Region barely moved.

items.title: We read college football's first 19 games: losers account for 17% of Q1 scoring and 39% of Q4
items.summary: The box score's final margin compresses the story. In the 10 games decided by halftime, the trailing team held just 5% of first-quarter points — and 39% of fourth-quarter points.

items.title: The CFPB logged 5.4 million complaints in 2025 — nine in ten about credit reporting, and 1 in 208 resolved with money
items.summary: As filing volume grew 6.8 times from 2022 to 2025, the share of complaints closed with any form of relief fell from 51 percent in 2024 to 41 percent in 2025

items.title: The world set a goal to protect 17% of its land and inland waters by 2020. Most economies with data fall below the line.
items.summary: Aichi Target 11 named a single global figure — 17% of terrestrial and inland-water areas — and a single deadline at Nagoya in 2010. By the land-area measure, most economies with data sit below it.

items.title: The world set one tobacco target — cut adult smoking 30% by 2025. On the WHO's own estimates it will miss, and the low-income countries, not the rich ones, are the bloc that already cleared the bar
items.summary: 194 governments endorsed the goal in 2013. We read the WHO's modeled prevalence for all 140 economies over a million people: 48 hit the 30% cut and 14 saw smoking rise — and the low-income group beat the target as a bloc while the upper-middle-income world lags furthest behind.

items.title: We read every 2025 QB run: scrambles made 80% of the rushing yards, designed runs 60% of the touchdowns
items.summary: The 38 quarterbacks who threw 200-plus passes ran for 8,801 yards and 97 touchdowns. Split every carry into a play the offense called and a scramble off a broken pass, and the two halves point opposite ways — Patrick Mahomes gained 420 of his 429 rushing yards improvising; Josh Allen scored 11 of his 14 rushing touchdowns on runs that were called.

items.title: The world's highest murder rates don't track national income: across 144 economies over a million people, Latin America and the Caribbean runs a median 12.6 homicides per 100,000 — seven times the rest of the world — and its deadliest are middle-income
items.summary: In 2015 every UN member pledged under Target 16.1 to reduce violent death 'everywhere.' We read the World Bank's latest homicide rate for every economy: national income barely sorts the ranking (correlation -0.20), and the top of it is upper-middle-income Latin America, not the poorest countries.

items.title: We read all 15 WNBA shot diets: three-point volume barely tracks a team's record; accuracy tracks it far more
items.summary: Across the full 2026 season to date, the share of a team's shots that come from three-point range is essentially unrelated to its record (Pearson 0.06, tie-aware Spearman 0.04) — the four most three-reliant offenses are 28-11, 24-16, 16-23 and 11-29. Three-point accuracy tracks winning far more closely (0.61 / 0.63); volume does not.

items.title: All 32 passing offenses: a lead pass-catcher's fantasy value tracked target concentration more closely than pass volume
items.summary: Rank all 32 NFL offenses by the share of targets its single busiest pass-catcher commanded and the lead receiver's full-PPR points follow it — correlation 0.74, against 0.38 for how many passes the team threw. Buffalo charged more targets than New Orleans and produced no startable receiver; New Orleans funneled 27.6% to Chris Olave and made him a WR6.

items.title: Two par-5s made nearly half the Tour Championship's under-par scoring — the other 16 holes played almost even
items.summary: Through 54 holes at East Lake, we scored every player who finished all three rounds: the 6th and 18th holes, 11% of the course, produced 112 of the field's 231 strokes under par — one shy of what all twelve par-4s made combined, at a 63.8% birdie rate.

items.title: The US says it shipped $334 billion of goods to Mexico in 2024; Mexico says it received $263 billion — a $71 billion gap that runs the wrong way, and has widened every year since 2021
items.summary: We read both governments' filings to UN Comtrade for 2021-2024. On goods heading north the two ledgers agree within about 1%. On goods heading south the importer records a fifth less than the exporter ships — the opposite of what freight costs predict — and the hole grew every year: $55B, $58B, $61B, $71B from 2021 to 2024.

items.title: Four currencies tripped the U.S. Treasury's 10-percent revaluation tripwire this quarter — and the biggest jump was a rate that had not moved in a decade
items.summary: The Treasury Reporting Rates of Exchange is the standard table federal agencies use to convert their foreign-currency transactions into dollars — amended mid-quarter only when a currency moves 10 percent or more. We read all 171 lines of the June 30 report: four carry an amendment, and Bolivia's boliviano — near 6.85 since 2016 — jumped to 10.35.

items.title: The rate-cut fight, checked against the data: inflation is still above 2% on every gauge the Fed watches — including headline PCE, the measure its formal 2% target is set on — and in July the job market started to shrink. The two halves of the Fed's mandate now pull opposite ways
items.summary: One camp says hold higher until inflation breaks; the other says cut before a softening labor market cracks. We pulled the numbers the argument turns on. Inflation is above the 2% goal on both the headline PCE gauge the Fed targets and the core reading it forecasts with — so the 'inflation is beaten' case isn't in the data. But July payrolls turned negative and the prior two months were revised down by 103,000, giving the cut side its own hard evidence. This is a genuine dual-mandate conflict, not a lean.

items.title: The EU writes two numbers into its own treaties — debt under 60% of GDP, deficit under 3%. On its 2024 books, 16 of 27 members breach at least one, and only 11 clear both
items.summary: We read Eurostat's own excessive-deficit filings for all 27 members. Twelve exceed the debt ceiling, eleven the deficit limit — but only seven breach both, and the biggest debtors are rarely the biggest deficit-runners. Greece carries the bloc's largest debt, 154% of GDP, and still ran a surplus.

items.title: Trump says he'll let ranchers 'process their own food.' They already can — the rule that stops them selling it is a federal inspection law only Congress can change
items.summary: The president named a real problem: four companies buy roughly 85% of U.S. fed cattle. His fix — 'legal documents' giving ranchers the right to process their own beef. A rancher's reply named the gap: that right already exists, but the meat is stamped 'Not For Sale.' We read the actual law. Each side is right about a different half.

items.title: We read all 49 workhorse backs of 2025: rushing touchdowns tracked goal-line carries, not total volume
items.summary: Across every running back who carried 100-plus times, rushing scores correlated 0.885 with carries inside the 10-yard line and just 0.636 with total carries — and in Seattle and Atlanta the back who owned the goal line was not the one who owned the workload.

items.title: For years the Social Security surplus made the federal deficit look smaller — through 10 months of fiscal 2026 the off-budget accounts added $116 billion to it instead
items.summary: Treasury's own books split the deficit in two, and the off-budget half — Social Security's trust funds and the Postal Service — has swung from a $6 billion surplus in fiscal 2022 to a $116 billion deficit, widening 44% in the past year

items.title: The developing world's debt service climbed from 8.1% to 12.4% of export earnings in a decade — and across the 114 economies the World Bank scores, the heaviest loads sit on middle-income borrowers, not the poorest
items.summary: We read every economy on the UN's debt-sustainability gauge for 2023. Twenty-eight now spend a fifth or more of what they export servicing external debt — yet low-income countries' median, 10.5%, sits below both middle-income tiers. On this gauge the debt load does not deepen with poverty.

items.title: The U.S. and New Zealand rate the same 204 countries for danger. They agree on 153 — and where they split, the U.S. is the stricter one nearly 3 to 1
items.summary: We read both governments' full advisory registers at once and lined them up country by country. The disagreements are not random: the extra U.S. caution lands almost entirely on Africa and the Caribbean, while the two capitals' 'Do Not Travel' lists — the gravest call a government makes — differ on just four places.

items.title: Two of MLB's three best records in one-run games belong to losing teams — close games barely track quality
items.summary: We split all 550 one-run games this season from the rest. Run differential tracks a team's multi-run record (r=0.92) and barely its one-run record (r=0.23) — Texas and Cincinnati sit top-three in close games with badly negative run margins.

items.title: One title holds nearly a fifth of the entire federal rulebook — environmental regulation, bigger than the 27 smallest CFR titles combined
items.summary: We measured all 49 active titles of the Code of Federal Regulations by the size the eCFR records for each. The code totals about 830 MB of regulatory text; Title 40 alone is 19.3% of it and 1.8x the next-largest — and over the past year the whole code moved less than 1%.

items.title: Field goals nearly matched touchdowns across the NFL preseason's first 33 games — and in six, the winner made no more touchdowns than the team it beat, but more field goals
items.summary: We counted every scoring play in the 33 completed games — Hall of Fame weekend plus the first two preseason weekends: 112 field goals against 123 touchdowns, a third of the kicks from 50 yards or longer, and in 6 of the 32 decided games the winner scored no more touchdowns than the team it beat. Two of the six were Tennessee's, both with four Joey Slye field goals.

items.title: The Fed's balance sheet is $2.235 trillion smaller than its 2022 peak — and bank reserves absorbed less than half the drop. The reverse-repo liability line gave up the most, $1.714 trillion, and the overnight facility inside it has drained to $175 million
items.summary: We read all 229 weekly Fed balance-sheet releases since the April 2022 peak and traced where the runoff came out. Of the $2.235 trillion in assets shed, the reverse-repo liability line gave up the largest single share — $1.714 trillion, 77% — while reserves fell $899 billion (40%) and the Treasury's cash balance and currency both rose. The overnight facility inside that line has drained to $175 million; the Fed concluded its runoff on Dec. 1, 2025, citing money-market signs that reserves had finally tightened.

items.title: Jefferson drew 19 red-zone targets and scored twice; Goedert drew 15 and scored 11 — we read all 811 receiving TDs
items.summary: In the 2025 regular season a target from inside the 20 scored at 24.2%, one from anywhere else at 1.6% — and across 124 pass-catchers the red-zone look, not the raw target column, is the target that tracks the scoring.

items.title: Nineteen countries the U.S. rates at its two lowest travel-risk tiers each hide a formal 'Do Not Travel' zone — and Georgia, rated at the scale's very lowest, is one
items.summary: We read all 215 advisories the State Department publishes at once. The single top-level rating is a destination-wide floor, not the local reality: 19 of the 164 countries and areas badged Level 1 or 2 carry a 'Do Not Travel To' region in their text.

items.title: The world pledged electricity for everyone by 2030. On its own 2024 numbers 655 million people are still without it — and among the 210 countries that report both rates, 83% of the unpowered live in the countryside
items.summary: We read the World Bank's 2024 access figures for all 215 reporting economies. Access is nearly universal in the cities — 98% globally — and the shortfall has collapsed onto the village: DR Congo reaches 55% of its urban residents and 1% of its rural ones, and eight countries hold half the people still in the dark.

items.title: 42 economies shrank in 2024 — and 17 of them recorded more births than deaths. Fertility does not cleanly sort the declines; the pattern is consistent with net outward movement
items.summary: We read every economy's own vital statistics: 7 of the 42 shrinking economies have fertility at or above replacement, while the famous low-fertility giants — China, Italy, Thailand — sit at the shallow end of the decline, not the steep one.

items.title: We read every US Open qualifying opener: the first-set winner won 84% of matches — and exactly half the deciders
items.summary: Across all 128 completed first-round qualifying matches at the 2026 US Open — 64 men, 64 women — the player who won the opening set won the match 105 of 125 times that finished on court. But that entire edge is straight-sets. Once a match reached a third set, the first-set winner went 20-20.

items.title: Read all $8.3 trillion in federal obligations by what the money buys: 72.6% is grants, benefits and interest, 11.5% is the government's own payroll
items.summary: Through three quarters of fiscal 2026 the government obligated more to outside contractual services and supplies than to its entire workforce — and six times as much to grants and fixed charges. The largest thing it does is move money, not make or hire.

items.title: A widely cited benchmark asks governments to spend 5% of GDP on health. Of 192 economies with 2022 data, 141 miss it — and the 30 high-income economies among them cannot be read simply as evidence of inability to pay
items.summary: Switzerland runs health through mandatory private insurance and covers barely a third of its own bill; the Gulf's petro-states fund most of theirs but divide by a hydrocarbon-heavy GDP — while Lesotho and Namibia clear a line set by how much a government spends on health relative to its GDP, not simply by national wealth.

items.title: We read all 36 qualified 2025 passers: 38% to 64% of each one's passing yards came after the catch
items.summary: Standard fantasy scoring pays 0.04 points a passing yard whether the quarterback drove it downfield or dumped it to a receiver who ran the rest. Jared Goff and Matthew Stafford each threw for about 4,600 yards in 2025 — Goff's came 53% after the catch, Stafford's 39%.

items.title: Outside the Postal Service, the federal workforce shed 165,000 jobs in one month — then all but stopped shrinking for six months
items.summary: We read every monthly federal payroll print since 1939. The 2025–26 downsizing was a single October cliff, not a glide — and by July 2026 it had held roughly flat for half a year, at the fewest civilian federal workers since 2009.

items.title: One UN road-safety target fell due in 2020, not 2030 — halve road deaths. We read WHO's rate estimates for the 183 economies it models: 13 halved their road-death rate, 71 got worse, and the global rate fell 8%
items.summary: SDG target 3.6 set a rare 2020 deadline. Measured 2010 to 2019, the deepest cuts were concentrated in Gulf and Central Asian economies that started with high death rates — while Western Europe, generally starting far lower, largely did not halve, and the United States moved the wrong way, 11.7 to 12.7 per 100,000.

items.title: The Federal Register shed 39% of its pages in 2025 but only 14% of its documents — its output fell far more in length than in count — and 2026 has won back about half the pages
items.summary: Read by the same Aug. 25 cutoff every year, the Register printed 68,242 pages in 2024, 41,501 in 2025 — its second-lowest count in a decade, behind only 2017 — and 54,935 in 2026. The document count barely tracked the swing: 18,766, then 16,140, then 16,949. Average pages per document fell from 3.64 to 2.57 and back to 3.24, while notices held a flat ~81% share throughout.

items.title: We read all 33 NFL preseason games so far: scoring peaks in the second quarter and craters in the third
items.summary: The fourth quarter, played almost entirely by backups, outscored the starters' opening quarter by 78 points. The scoring doesn't follow the talent off the field.

items.title: We priced all 31,210 fantasy opportunities of 2025: in PPR a target is worth 2.64 carries, 1.60 in standard
items.summary: A carry and a target are the two atoms of fantasy scoring, and they are not priced alike. Read the complete 2025 ledger and the gap holds even inside the running-back pool — the 55 backs with 100-plus opportunities ran on 81% of their chances but banked only 63% of their points there, and made the other 37% on the 19% that came through the air.

items.title: Read by function, not by agency, the second-largest increase in federal spending through July was interest
items.summary: We pulled the Monthly Treasury Statement's functional ledger, which files spending by purpose rather than by department. Of 19 budget functions, net interest added $90.6 billion year-over-year — the largest increase of any function except Medicare, and more than Social Security, defense or veterans' care. The department ledger hides it inside Treasury; this one puts it on its own line.

items.title: The UN's child-survival goal wrote two floors, not one. Read all 196 economies' 2023 estimates and the newborn floor is the one that traps the near-winners — 9 clear the under-5 line but miss it, to just 3 the other way
items.summary: 120 economies clear both the 25-per-1,000 under-5 threshold and the 12-per-1,000 neonatal one; 64 clear neither. But of the dozen that split, every one of the nine still short on newborns has already beaten the child floor — the first 28 days is the harder half.

items.title: The UK updated 206 of its 226 travel-advice pages on one December day with the same sentence — and for 38 countries it is still the newest change
items.summary: Read one country page and the update date looks like fresh local intelligence. Read all 226 at once and it resolves into a single note about British dual nationals, pasted across the world in a day — the third time since 2020 one sentence has landed on 200-plus pages at once.

items.title: The Federal Reserve sent the Treasury about $88 billion a year for the better part of a decade. Since September 2022 it has sent almost nothing — and its own balance sheet carries a $233 billion reason why.
items.summary: Treasury's receipt line for Federal Reserve earnings collapsed from $106.7 billion in fiscal 2022 to $0.58 billion the next year. The Fed's own books explain it: a 'deferred asset' — the losses it must earn back before payments resume — that grew for more than three years to $245.9 billion, peaked in January 2026, and has only just begun to shrink.

items.title: The UN has told the least developed countries to grow 7% a year since 2001. We read all 44's own national accounts: in 2024, 4 cleared it — and across the whole decade only one averaged it
items.summary: Ethiopia is the sole LDC whose 2015-2024 growth averaged the target. Not one of the 44 posted 7% in every year it reported, and across the decade the group never reached the line — it peaked at 4.8% in 2019 and sat at 3.9% in 2024.

items.title: The average WR week overstates the typical one: rank 2025's top 36 by median, not mean, and 16 move five-plus spots
items.summary: We scored all 18 regular-season weeks in full PPR for every receiver who played at least 14 of them. For 78 of 94, the season average sat above the median game — a few booms lifting a number a weekly lineup never collects. Michael Wilson ranked WR13 by average and WR35 by the game he turned in half the time.

items.title: The 119th Congress has introduced 18,433 measures — we counted every one, and 2,491 of them, about one in seven, belong to categories that can never become law
items.summary: Bills and joint resolutions can be signed into law; the 153 concurrent and 2,338 simple resolutions cannot, by the Constitution's own design. Of the 15,942 bills and joint resolutions, 102 have made it into the statute books — about 1 in 156 — and the simple resolutions alone outnumber the enacted laws by more than 22 to 1.

items.title: The UN set 2020 to bring the least-developed countries universal internet. In the deadline year 24% of their people were online — and across the 37 with 2023 data, the median country is still majority-offline
items.summary: The World Bank's own series puts the LDC average at 31% in 2024 — below the level the world as a whole had already passed in 2015, while high-income economies sit at 93%. None of the 37 reporting LDCs has reached universal; use runs from Burundi's 7% to Kiribati's 88%.
